doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Engaging the audience and crediting composers
summary: He urges musicians to talk to audiences and name composers, citing Buster Williams and Stephon Harris.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: See that comes, I think your sensitivity to that also is partly due to the fact that you do write, you know, so that you feel like composers should be acknowledged when they get their pieces played, and that’s on target.

Yeah. I mean I heard a concert where Buster Williams was playing. And he has this incredible piece called “Christina.” It’s one of the most beautiful ballads you ever want to hear. But he was a side man in this one group. They did it. You didn’t know the name of the song, let alone know that Buster wrote it. And I think in a room full of people it might be nice to know that it wasn’t written by a piano player, it wasn’t written by a horn player, but this beautifully harmonically intricate song was written by the bass player who happens to be on the stage right now. How do we get to know our new composers? How do we get to know these guys? Okay? Not just that Buster is a great bass player, but © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

he’s a great composer at the same time. And this bothers me in the music. The lack of concern for the audience. And you don’t have to become shuckin’ and jivin’ all kinds of stuff, but just engage, to communicate. I remember Stephon Harris who is one of the brightest young vibraphonist musicians out there. I remember going to his gig. And he was getting ready to announce the song and he couldn’t remember the tune. And he played it up. He had everybody cracking up. Because he’s getting ready to play the song, he doesn’t even know the title of his own tune, and everybody’s like cracking up in the club, which is part of the whole thing. And then he said, “I got this other tune I wrote, and you know something, I don’t have a title for it so I’ll tell you what, if any of you have a good idea for a title, please let me know.” Do you know people came up to the stage and said, “Stephon, I got the title for you man.” You know it was great because you were engaging the audience. Okay? We don’t have to go jumping around, everybody’s not going like hey, all right. You know? You don’t want that. But still in talking and communicating, because what happens is, this is my own feeling, what happens is that when you go to see a musician play, you come away with one or two things. “Man he was bad man, hey man, he plays his butt off.” Or “he was kind of sad, you know, I wasn’t really feeling him.” To me that’s very one or two dimensional at best. You don’t know whether they have a sense of humor, you don’t know whether they have kids, they’re married, if they have any views. Which many times you see so many songs, like especially like say during apartheid, you get all these songs, “Johannesburg,” “Soweto,” “Tutu.” But no one talked about the inspiration with these songs. You know it just became a tune that showed that they knew what was going on in the world. But not so much to have any thought about it. Just that it made them current. Well why don’t we hear some views that you have about South Africa? About apartheid? Okay? We don’t do that. And a lot of musicians did and still do talk, engage, that’s what Cannonball did, Duke did, Louis Armstrong did, Barry Harris does. Okay? There are a lot of musicians who do talk. Frank Foster does, okay. So it’s not an indictment against all of us. But there are enough of us that do not engage the audience that just makes it like one dimensional.
